claims.text: The spec names four roles: the resource owner (you), the client (the app), the authorization server (issues the keys) and the resource server (hosts the data).
An access token is a string that represents an authorization issued to the client.
Whoever holds a bearer token can use it; they don't have to prove they own any key.
Clients send the token in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme: Authorization: Bearer followed by the token.
The spec says bearer tokens should not be passed in page URLs, because URLs end up in places like browser history and logs.
The authorization request carries response_type=code and client_id, and usually redirect_uri, scope and state.
PKCE adds two parameters to that request: code_challenge and code_challenge_method.
The spec says the code must expire shortly after it is issued and recommends a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes.
The client must not use an authorization code more than once.
If a code is used more than once, the login server must deny the request.
RFC 9700 says clients should not use the implicit grant (response type token), because access tokens returned in the redirect can leak and be replayed.
RFC 9700 was published in January 2025 as a Best Current Practice.
PKCE was designed against an attack where a malicious app on the same device intercepts the code meant for the real app.
The app makes a code_verifier: a random string of 43 to 128 characters drawn from letters, digits and the symbols - . _ ~.
With the S256 method, the code_challenge is BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)).
At the token endpoint the server transforms the code_verifier and compares it with the stored challenge; if they differ, it returns an invalid_grant error.
RFC 9700 notes that PKCE was designed to protect native apps, but its advice now applies to all kinds of clients, including web applications.
RFC 9700 says public clients must use PKCE and recommends it for confidential clients too.
Clients should use S256, currently the only PKCE method that doesn't expose the verifier in the authorization request.
Authorization servers must support PKCE and must reject a token request with a code_verifier when the authorization request carried no code_challenge.
If code_challenge_method is left out, it defaults to plain, where the challenge is the verifier itself.
Refresh tokens are used only with the authorization server and are never sent to resource servers.
The client exchanges a refresh token at the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token, and the server may issue a new refresh token at the same time.
The spec splits clients into confidential clients, which can keep a secret (typically server-side apps), and public clients, which can't (native apps and apps running in the browser).
For public clients, RFC 9700 requires refresh tokens to be sender-constrained or rotated.
Rotation means every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the previous one.

claims.text: The token request sends grant_type=authorization_code and the code, plus the redirect_uri if the first request had one, and with PKCE the code_verifier; a client that doesn't authenticate also sends its client_id.

claims.text: RFC 9068 says a JWT access token must declare itself in its typ header, normally as at+jwt, which lets APIs tell it apart from other JWTs such as ID tokens.

checks.note: reviewer flagged wording; sentence corrected and re-checked

claims.text: The resource server must check that typ is at+jwt, that iss exactly matches the expected issuer, that aud contains its own identifier, that the signature is valid, and that exp is in the future, and must reject tokens with alg none.

claims.text: Required claims in a JWT access token are iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti.
If scopes were requested, the token should carry them in a scope claim.
When a token is rejected, the error invalid_token goes with HTTP 401 and insufficient_scope with HTTP 403.
PyJWT's documentation warns never to build the algorithms list from the token's own alg header.
RFC 9700 requires PKCE for public clients and recommends it for all others.
The client credentials grant is for a client acting on resources it controls or has pre-arranged access to, and only confidential clients may use it.
The device authorization grant is for devices that have no browser or can't easily take input, such as smart TVs and printers.
Native apps must send the authorization request through an external user-agent such as the system browser, not an embedded web view.
While polling, the error authorization_pending means keep polling and slow_down means poll less often.
GitHub documents the device flow for headless apps such as CLI tools, and in its web flow supports PKCE with S256 only.
RFC 9700 says the resource owner password credentials grant must not be used.
Authorization servers must compare redirect URIs by exact string match; the only exception is the port of a localhost redirect for native apps.
Clients and authorization servers must not expose open redirectors, pages that forward the browser to any URL given in a query parameter.
Clients must prevent CSRF, either with a one-time state value bound to the user's browser or by relying on PKCE when the authorization server is known to support it.
Such a client should use the iss response parameter to tell the servers apart, or failing that, a distinct redirect URI per server.
RFC 9700 allows a client to rely on PKCE for CSRF protection once it has ensured the login server supports PKCE.
In April 2022, attackers used OAuth user tokens stolen from two GitHub integrators, Heroku and Travis CI, to list and clone private repositories of dozens of organisations.

GitHub spotted it when a compromised AWS key was used to access npm's production infrastructure; it revoked the tokens tied to its own use of the affected apps and asked Heroku and Travis CI to revoke all the others.

claims.text: RFC 9700 says access tokens should be audience-restricted to a specific resource server and limited to the privileges needed.
RFC 9700 says authorization and resource servers should use sender-constrained access tokens, through mutual TLS (RFC 8705) or DPoP (RFC 9449).
The revocation endpoint takes a token by POST, and revoking a refresh token should also invalidate the access tokens issued from the same grant, if the server supports that.

With DPoP the client signs a small proof JWT for each request with its private key; the proof names the HTTP method and URL, includes a hash of the access token when calling an API, and travels in a DPoP header.

claims.text: With token introspection the API POSTs the token to the authorization server, which answers with JSON whose required active field says whether the token is currently valid.
RFC 7662 describes the caching trade-off: a longer cache cuts load on the introspection endpoint, but a revoked token can stay usable until the cache entry expires.
For local checks, the authorization server can publish its signing keys at a jwks_uri listed in its metadata, and RFC 9068 says it should do so for resource servers.

claims.text: By default that metadata lives at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server on the issuer's host, placed before any path the issuer URL has.

claims.text: PyJWT's decode function takes a leeway argument that allows a small margin when checking expiry, for clocks that are slightly out of sync.
OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0; OAuth by itself does not tell the app who the user is or how they authenticated.
An OpenID Connect request must include openid in its scope.
OpenID Connect adds the ID token, a JWT whose required claims include iss, sub, aud, exp and iat, with aud including the client's ID.

claims.text: RFC 10017 (August 2026), on browser-based apps, strongly recommends the Backend for Frontend pattern for business applications, sensitive applications and apps that handle personal data.
In a BFF a server-side component acts as the confidential OAuth client and keeps the tokens, so there are no tokens in the browser to steal.
RFC 10017 notes one attack remains: someone who hijacks the app inside the user's browser can still act through it, a problem inherent to web applications.
RFC 6749 is still the core OAuth 2.0 spec; RFC 8252, RFC 8996 and RFC 9700 update it.
OAuth 2.1, which folds these best practices into one document meant to replace RFC 6749 and RFC 6750, is still an IETF working-group draft as of September 2026.
RFC 9700 recommends asymmetric client authentication, such as mutual TLS or signed JWTs with a private key, over shared secrets.
